title.text: Probability basics: random variables, independence, expectation, variance and covariance

objects.text: A chat model gives every possible next word a probability. What does that number mean, and why do they all add up to exactly one?

Mathematics for AI and Machine Learning  |  Session 13 of 18  |  Probability and statistics
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes: Welcome to Session 13, and to the third pillar of the course: probability and statistics. Everything so far gave us numbers. From today we deal with chance, which is what a language model faces every time it must pick the next word. Today is the vocabulary: random variables, independence, expectation, variance and covariance. We use dice, a small next-word list and a small dataset.

title.text: Today in one view: what you will leave with

objects.text: By the end of today you can

objects.alt: book

objects.text: Describe a sample space, an event, a random variable and independence, and use the rules of probability on dice

objects.alt: calculator

objects.text: Calculate an expectation, a variance, a standard deviation, a covariance and a correlation by hand and by computer, and say whether a list is divided by n or n - 1

objects.alt: chart

objects.text: Read a next-word probability list from a chat model as a probability mass function

slides.notes:
Three things to take away today. You can describe a sample space, an event, a random variable and what it means for two of them to be independent, and you can use the rules of probability on dice. You can calculate an expectation, a variance, a standard deviation, a covariance and a correlation, first by hand and then by computer, and you can say whether a list of data was divided by n or by n minus one.

And you can read the list of next-word probabilities that a chat model produces as a probability mass function, which answers the question on the first slide.

title.text:
Your two hours: dice and data
first, then the lab, then AI

objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: Pictures and hand calculations first. Then the lab on dice, next-word probabilities and a small dataset.

slides.notes:
We start with ten minutes of recall from Session 12, and the question about next-word probabilities. Then thirty-five minutes of concepts, always a picture first and then one example by hand. After the break you spend forty-five minutes in the lab, in Python or in a spreadsheet, on the same numbers.

We finish by seeing where this appears in AI, with an exit check, and then you save your work.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  Why can computing e to the power of a large score break a softmax, and what does the stable softmax do about it?
2.  What does regularisation (an L2 penalty, also called weight decay) add to the loss, and why?
3.  Many models use 16-bit numbers. What is the saving and what is the risk?

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 12. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. Why can computing e to the power of a large score break a softmax, and what does the stable softmax do about it? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. The number overflows (too large for the computer). The stable softmax subtracts the largest score first. The probabilities stay the same.

Question two. What does regularisation (an L2 penalty, also called weight decay) add to the loss, and why? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. A penalty that grows with the size of the weights. It keeps weights small and reduces overfitting.

Question three. Many models use 16-bit numbers. What is the saving and what is the risk? Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. Less memory and less time. The largest number in the 16-bit floating-point format fp16 is only 65,504, so overflow comes sooner (bfloat16 keeps the range but loses precision).

If an answer was missing, do not worry. Your notes from last class have it. Now to today.

title.text: Answers to the three questions from Session 12

rows.text: Why can computing e to the power of a large score break a softmax, and what does the stable softmax do about it?
The number overflows (too large for the computer). The stable softmax subtracts the largest score first. The probabilities stay the same.
What does regularisation (an L2 penalty, also called weight decay) add to the loss, and why?
A penalty that grows with the size of the weights. It keeps weights small and reduces overfitting.
Many models use 16-bit numbers. What is the saving and what is the risk?
Less memory and less time. The largest number in the 16-bit floating-point format fp16 is only 65,504, so overflow comes sooner (bfloat16 keeps the range but loses precision).

objects.text: If one answer surprised you, look back at Session 12 before the lab.

slides.notes:
Three short answers. First, a large score overflows when we take e to its power. The stable softmax subtracts the largest score first, and the probabilities do not change. Second, regularisation adds a penalty that grows with the weights, so they stay small and overfitting is reduced. Third, 16-bit numbers save memory and time, but in the fp16 format they top out at 65,504, so overflow comes sooner and the stable softmax matters more.

The bfloat16 format keeps the range but loses precision. Check your own answers against these.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Random variable. A rule that turns the outcome of a chance event into a number. We write it X.

Independent random variables. Knowing the value of one does not change the probabilities of the other, like two separate dice.

Probability mass function (pmf) and density function (pdf). The pmf gives P(X = x) for values you can list. The pdf is a curve, and probability is the area under it.

Expectation, variance and standard deviation. The probability-weighted average mu, the average squared distance from it, and its square root sigma.

title.text:
A sample space lists every outcome,
and an event is a group of outcomes

objects.alt: A sample space lists every outcome, and an event is a group of outcomes

objects.text: Two fair dice give 36 equally likely outcomes. Each cell shows the sum.

runs.text: Sample space: all possible outcomes.
Event: a group of outcomes. Gold = "sum is 7".
P(sum is 7) = 6/36, about 0.167. A probability runs from 0 to 1.

slides.notes:
Roll two fair dice. Each cell in this table is one outcome, and the number inside is the sum of the two dice. There are thirty-six cells, and they are equally likely. The set of all outcomes is called the sample space. An event is any group of outcomes we care about, and the gold cells are the event that the sum is seven.

A probability is a number from zero, impossible, to one, certain. When outcomes are equally likely it is the count in the event over the count of all outcomes: six over thirty-six, one sixth, about 0.167. Count the cells for a sum of 10 and you get three.

title.text: The rules of probability, checked on dice

objects.alt: The rules of probability, checked on dice

rows.text: Two events. A = the die is even {2, 4, 6}. B = the die shows more than 4 {5, 6}.
Both at once: only the face 6.
At least one: 2, 4, 5, 6. The 6 is counted once, so we subtract it once.

objects.text: Complement example: P(not even) = 1 - 3/6 = 3/6. The six faces of one die, 1/6 each, add up to 1.

slides.notes:
Four rules, each checked on a single die. The probability is never below zero or above one, and all outcomes together have probability one. That last rule answers half of today's question: something must happen, so the probabilities of every possible next word add to one. The probability that A does not happen is one minus the probability that it does.

For either one of two events, add their probabilities and subtract the overlap, because the overlap was counted twice. Take A as even and B as more than four. The six belongs to both, so three sixths plus two sixths minus one sixth gives four sixths. Check by listing 2, 4, 5, 6.

title.text:
A random variable turns each outcome into a
number, and its pmf says how likely each number is

objects.alt: A random variable turns each outcome into a number, and its pmf says how likely each number is

objects.text: Let X be the sum of two dice. The bar heights are the probability mass function (pmf): p(x) = P(X = x).

runs.text: A random variable X gives a number to each outcome.
P(X = 7) = 6/36 is the tallest bar (gold).
All the bars add up to 1.

slides.notes:
A random variable is a rule that gives a number to every outcome of a chance event. Here X is the sum of two dice, so X can be any whole number from two to twelve. The heights of the bars are the probability mass function, the pmf: for each value x, the probability that X equals x.

Seven is the tallest because six of the thirty-six outcomes give it. Two and twelve are the shortest, one outcome each. Add all eleven bars and you get thirty-six over thirty-six, which is one. Read P(X = 2) off the first bar: one thirty-sixth.

title.text:
Two random variables are independent when knowing
one does not change the probabilities of the other

objects.alt: Two random variables are independent when knowing one does not change the probabilities of the other

objects.text: X₁ = die 1, X₂ = die 2. Independent: P(X₁ = a and X₂ = b) = P(X₁ = a) × P(X₂ = b) for every pair a, b.

runs.text: Pale: a 6 on one die. Gold: both show 6.
Die 1 and the sum are dependent: die 1 = 1 rules out a sum of 12.

slides.notes:
Two random variables are independent when knowing the value of one tells you nothing new about the other. Two separate dice are the standard example. The first die landing on six does not change the chances of the second. In symbols, the probability of both values is the product of the two probabilities, for every pair of values.

Check the gold cell: one cell in thirty-six, and one sixth times one sixth is one thirty-sixth. Compare die one with the sum of the dice. If die one shows a one, a sum of twelve becomes impossible, so those two are dependent. Sessions 14 and 15 lean on this idea again and again.

title.text:
A continuous random variable has a density
curve, and probability is the area under it

objects.alt: A continuous random variable has a density curve, and probability is the area under it

objects.text: A bus arrives at a random moment in a 10 minute window. This is a uniform distribution: every moment is equally likely.

runs.text: Density f(x) (pdf): the curve, flat at 1/10 = 0.1, so total area = 10 × 0.1 = 1.
P(2 to 5 minutes) = width 3 × height 0.1 = 0.3.
P(exactly 3.000...) = 0. Only ranges have probability.

slides.notes:
Some random variables take values that cannot be listed. The waiting time for a bus, in a ten minute window, can be any value, so we call it continuous, and we cannot draw one bar per value. Instead we draw a density curve, the probability density function, the pdf.

The height of the curve is not a probability. The area under the curve between two values is. Here the curve is flat at 0.1, so the area between two and five minutes is three times 0.1, which is 0.3. The probability of one exact instant is zero.

This flat curve is called a uniform distribution, and its total area is ten times 0.1, which is one. The numbers are illustrative.

title.text:
Probability mass function and
density function, side by side

objects.alt: Probability mass function and density function, side by side

rows.text: The probability that X takes exactly the value x. Never negative.
The density: the height of the curve at x. It can be above 1.
Sigma (Session 1): add over every value x that X can take.
Integral: the area under f from a to b. dx: along the x axis.

objects.text: Both say the total probability is 1. Values you can list use a sum, a continuous curve uses an area.

slides.notes:
The two descriptions side by side. For discrete values, which you can list, we have the pmf, written p of x, the probability that X equals x. The sigma sign from Session 1 adds it over every value x, and the total must be one. For a continuous variable we have the density f of x, and the probability that X lies between a and b is the area under the curve from a to b.

The tall S is the integral sign, and the dx at the end says the area runs along the x axis. You never calculate integrals by hand in this course. For flat curves the area is width times height.

title.text:
A chat model gives every possible next word
a probability, and the probabilities add up to 1

objects.alt: A chat model gives every possible next word a probability, and the probabilities add up to 1

objects.text: Illustrative (made-up numbers): next word after "For breakfast I drink hot ...".

runs.text: Logits z: one raw score per word.
Softmax (Session 12) turns the scores into probabilities.

slides.notes:
This is the answer to our question, with made-up numbers, so please treat them as illustrative. Suppose a model reads the start of a sentence, and it scores five candidate next words. These raw scores are called logits. Softmax, from Session 12, turns them into probabilities. Tea gets 0.446, coffee 0.299, and so on.

The list is a probability mass function. It is never negative, and it adds up to one, because the model must choose some word. A real model does this for every token in its vocabulary. Tea is the best bet, though it wins less than half the time.

title.text:
Expectation is the probability-weighted
average, the balance point of the bars

objects.alt: Expectation is the probability-weighted average, the balance point of the bars

objects.text: Expectation E(X), also called the mean and written mu, is the value the average settles on over many repeats.

runs.text: Picture the bars as weights on a ruler. E(X) is where it balances.
It need not be a possible value: no die shows 3.5.
No n here: each value is weighted by its probability p(x).

slides.notes:
Expectation answers the question: what would the average be if we repeated this chance event many times?

Put the bars on a ruler as weights. The expectation is the point where the ruler balances. For a fair die it is exactly in the middle, 3.5. You can never roll a 3.5. The expectation is an average over many rolls and says nothing certain about one roll.

Statisticians also call it the mean and write it mu. There is no count of rows here: each value is weighted by its probability. If the six had a heavier bar, the balance point would move to the right.

title.text:
Expectation: add up each
value times its probability

objects.alt: Expectation: add up each value times its probability

rows.text: The expectation (mean) of the random variable X.
One possible value of X, and its probability.
Any rule applied to the value, weighted by p(x).

objects.text: The last line is how losses are averaged in AI: g is the loss for one outcome, E(g(X)) is the expected loss.

slides.notes:
The formula says: multiply each possible value by its probability, and add. For the die each face has probability one sixth, so we get twenty-one sixths, which is 3.5. The third line is the same idea for any rule g applied to the value. Weight g of x by the probability and add.

With g of x equal to x squared, the die gives ninety-one sixths, about 15.17, which we need for the variance shortcut. Training a model averages a loss in exactly this way, as Sessions 16 and 17 show. The same formula works on the next word, too.

title.text:
Expected surprise of the next word: weight each
word's surprise by its probability, 1.309 nats

objects.alt: Expected surprise of the next word: weight each word's surprise by its probability, 1.309 nats

objects.text: Surprise g(x) = -ln p(x) (ln from Session 1): a likely word surprises little, a rare word a lot. Unit: nats, because we use ln.

runs.text: E(surprise) = sum of the last column = 1.3093 nats.
Session 17 calls this average surprise the entropy, and builds the training loss from it.

slides.notes:
An expectation with a real AI meaning. Give each word a surprise, minus the natural log of its probability. Tea, the likely word, has a small surprise of 0.81. Soup, the unlikely one, has 3.41. The expected surprise weights each surprise by its probability and adds. The last column sums to 1.3093.

With ln the unit is called a nat. Session 17 gives this average surprise its proper name, the entropy, and shows that a language model is trained by making the surprise of the real next word small. For today it is one more use of the same expectation formula. The numbers are illustrative.

title.text:
Variance and standard deviation measure
how far values lie from the mean

objects.alt: Variance and standard deviation measure how far values lie from the mean

rows.text: Variance: average squared distance from mu (units of X squared).
Standard deviation: the square root, in the units of X.
How far one value lies from the expectation.
The expectation of X squared: sum of x² times p(x).

objects.text: We square the distances so that below-mean and above-mean values do not cancel. Again no n: the weights are p(x).

slides.notes:
Expectation tells us the centre. Variance tells us the spread. For each value take its distance from the mean, square it, weight it by its probability, and add. We square so that values below and above the mean do not cancel each other. The standard deviation, sigma, is the square root of the variance, and it has the same units as X, which makes it easier to read.

The shortcut uses the expectation of X squared from the previous formula slide: 91 over 6 is 15.1667, minus 3.5 squared, 12.25, gives 2.9167. The direct route gives the same number, and we check it by hand.

title.text:
By hand: the variance of a
fair die is 35/12, about 2.92

objects.alt: By hand: the variance of a fair die is 35/12, about 2.92

objects.text: Each face has p(x) = 1/6, so add the last column and divide by 6.

runs.text: Sum of the last column = 17.50.
Standard deviation = square root = 1.7078: a root-mean-square distance from 3.5.

slides.notes:
The die by hand. Column one is the face. Column two is its distance from 3.5, and column three squares that distance. The ends, 1 and 6, are 2.5 away, and squared that gives 6.25. The middle faces are only half a unit away, which gives 0.25. Add the six squared distances and you get 17.5.

Every face has probability one sixth, so divide by six. The variance is 2.9167, and the standard deviation is 1.7078. The standard deviation is a root-mean-square distance from 3.5. The plain average distance is 1.5, a little smaller, because squaring gives the far faces more weight.

title.text:
A whole population divides
by n, and a sample by n - 1

objects.alt: check

objects.text: Sample: divide by n - 1

runs.text: Default since Session 5
np.var(x, ddof=1)
VAR.S, STDEV.S, COVARIANCE.S

objects.alt: flag

objects.text: Population: divide by n

runs.text: The list is all there is
np.var(x)
VAR.P, STDEV.P, COVARIANCE.P

objects.text: Distances from x̄ come out a little small; n - 1 corrects it. Var(y): 8.4 or 7.

slides.notes:
The die had known probabilities. A list of data does not, so give each of the n rows probability one over n. The expectation becomes the plain average, x bar, and the variance becomes the average squared distance, dividing by n. That is right when the list is the whole population.

Usually it is a sample, and the distances are measured from x bar, which was fitted to the same rows, so they come out slightly small. Dividing by n minus one corrects that. Session 5 divided by n minus one, and this course keeps that default for data and always says which.

In NumPy np.var divides by n unless you write ddof equals 1, while np.cov and pandas divide by n minus one unless told otherwise.

title.text:
Covariance asks whether two
columns rise and fall together

objects.alt: Covariance asks whether two columns rise and fall together

objects.text: Illustrative: six learners. Dashed red lines: the two means. Shaded corners: product above 0.

runs.text: Dark dot: both above or both below the means. Product positive.
Open dot: product negative.
Per learner: (x - x̄)(y - ȳ). Add, divide by n - 1. Session 5 put it in a matrix.

slides.notes:
Two columns at once. Six learners, with the hours they study per week across and the quiz score up. These numbers are illustrative. The two dashed lines are the means, and they cut the picture into four corners. A dark dot sits top right or bottom left: both values above average, or both below.

Those dots add positive amounts. For each learner we multiply the distance from the mean of x by the distance from the mean of y, then add the products and divide by n minus one, because six learners are a sample. An open dot pulls the total down.

You met this number in Session 5, off the diagonal of the covariance matrix.

title.text:
By hand: the sample covariance
of the six learners is 25 / 5 = 5

objects.alt: By hand: the sample covariance of the six learners is 25 / 5 = 5

objects.text: The means are x̄ = 4 hours and ȳ = 6 points. Multiply the two distances for every learner.

runs.text: Sample covariance = 25 / (6 - 1) = 5.
Sample variances: x 5.6, y 8.4.

slides.notes:
The hand calculation. The mean of x, written x bar, is four hours, and the mean of y, y bar, is six points. For each learner we take the distance from each mean and multiply the two. The first learner is three below on hours and two below on score, so the product is plus six.

The third learner studied little but scored high, so the product is minus two. The six products add to 25. Six learners are a sample, so divide by n minus one, five, and the covariance is 5. Two negative products keep it smaller than if every learner had moved together.

title.text:
Covariance and correlation: how
two columns move together

objects.alt: Covariance and correlation: how two columns move together

rows.text: Sum of the products of the two distances, divided by n - 1.
The sample standard deviations (also divide by n - 1).
Covariance divided by both standard deviations. No units, between -1 and +1.

objects.text: The n - 1 cancels top and bottom, so r is the same with either divisor. Cov of a column with itself is its variance.

slides.notes:
Two formulas. The sample covariance adds the products of the distances from the means and divides by n minus one, the same formula as Session 5. Its units are hours times points, which is hard to interpret. Correlation fixes that. Divide the covariance by both standard deviations and the units cancel.

The result always lies between minus one and plus one. For our six learners it is 0.729: a fairly strong positive link. The n minus one appears in the top and in the bottom, so it cancels, and r is the same whichever divisor you use. And the covariance of a column with itself is its variance, the diagonal of the Session 5 matrix.

title.text:
Correlation runs from -1 to 1, and
it only sees straight-line patterns

objects.alt: Correlation runs from -1 to 1, and it only sees straight-line patterns

objects.text: Each panel shows 40 made-up points and their correlation r.

runs.text: r near +1: the columns rise together.
r near -1: one rises as the other falls.
r near 0: no straight-line trend.

slides.notes:
Correlation as a picture. Forty made-up points in each panel. On the left the columns move in opposite directions, so r is close to minus one. In the middle the dots form a cloud with no trend, and r is near zero. On the right they rise together and r is close to plus one.

Correlation is a single number that summarises the straight-line trend. That is useful, and it is also its limit, as the next picture shows.

title.text:
Common mistake: a correlation near 0
does not mean the columns are unrelated

objects.alt: Common mistake: a correlation near 0 does not mean the columns are unrelated

objects.text: Both panels have r close to 0. Only the right one has no relationship.

runs.text: Correlation measures straight-line trends only.
A strong curve can still give r near 0.
High correlation does not prove that one column causes the other.

slides.notes:
A common mistake. Both of these panels have a correlation near zero. The right panel is a cloud with no pattern. The left panel has a perfect U shape, a very strong relationship, but no straight line. Correlation cannot see curves. So always draw the scatter plot before you trust the number.

One more caution: even a high correlation does not show that one column causes the other. Ice cream sales and sunburn both rise in summer. Which hidden factor links them?

title.text:
Bridge: expectation, variance,
covariance and correlation in NumPy

runs.text: import
numpy
as
np
np.mean(x), np.var(x, ddof=1), np.std(x, ddof=1)
np.cov(x, y)[0, 1]
np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1]

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: Lines 2 and 3: the two columns as arrays.
Line 4: mean, then sample variance and standard deviation. ddof=1 divides by n - 1.
Line 5: np.cov gives a 2 by 2 matrix and divides by n - 1. Row 0, column 1 is Cov(x, y).
Line 6: np.corrcoef gives the correlation matrix. Same entry is r.
Spreadsheet: AVERAGE, VAR.S, STDEV.S, COVARIANCE.S and CORREL.

slides.notes:
The same work in code. Two arrays, x and y. NumPy has mean, var and std. Without ddof equals one, var and std divide by n, so we add it to get the sample versions. For covariance we call np.cov. It divides by n minus one already, and it returns a small matrix, the covariance matrix of Session 5.

The covariance of x and y is the entry in row zero, column one. np.corrcoef gives the correlation matrix in the same shape. In the spreadsheet you use AVERAGE, VAR.S, STDEV.S, COVARIANCE.S and CORREL, and you see the same numbers in both tools.

title.text:
Bridge: simulate dice with a fixed
seed so everyone gets the same rolls

runs.text: rng = np.random.default_rng(13)
rolls = rng.integers(1, 7, size=60)
rolls.mean(), rolls.var(ddof=1)
rng = np.random.default_rng(13)
big = rng.integers(1, 7, size=10000)
big.mean(), big.var(ddof=1)

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: Line 1: a random number generator. Seed 13 fixes the sequence.
Line 2: 60 whole numbers from 1 to 6 (7 is excluded).
Line 3: 60 rolls give a noisy mean (3.9667) and sample variance (3.1853).
Lines 4 to 6: start the generator again; 10,000 rolls come much closer to 3.5 and 2.9167.
Spreadsheet: the 60 rolls are fixed values, so nothing changes.

slides.notes:
Simulation means letting the computer roll the dice for us. The generator with seed thirteen gives the same sequence on every machine, so your numbers match mine. The call integers from one to seven gives whole numbers from one to six, because the upper limit is not included.

Sixty rolls give a noisy mean, here 3.9667, and a sample variance of 3.1853. Line four starts the generator again from seed thirteen, as the notebook does, so your ten thousand rolls match your neighbour's. They come much closer to 3.5 and 2.9167. In the spreadsheet we paste fixed rolls, so the numbers stay put.

title.text:
Errors you will meet, what

title.text:
Where this appears in AI: a language
model gives every next token a probability

objects.alt: Where this appears in AI: a language model gives every next token a probability

objects.text: Language models of this kind output a probability mass function over the whole vocabulary.

runs.text: Published transformers end in a softmax over the vocabulary.
Llama 2 (open): 32,000 tokens in the vocabulary.
Closed products do not publish details.

slides.notes:
Today in real systems. The published transformer design ends with one score, a logit, for every token in its vocabulary. Softmax turns those scores into a probability mass function that adds to one. The open model Llama 2, for example, has a published vocabulary of 32,000 tokens. ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude are products built on models of this kind, but their exact details are not public.

So we use the published design and open models to show the same mathematics. Next session shows how a program draws one token from this list.

title.text:
Where this appears in AI: mean and standard
deviation rescale numbers inside the model

objects.alt: Where this appears in AI: mean and standard deviation rescale numbers inside the model

objects.text: The original transformer uses layer normalisation: each vector is centred and scaled with its own mean and standard deviation.

runs.text: Layer normalisation: Ba, Kiros and Hinton, 2016. It divides by n: the vector is the whole population.
Some newer open models use a variant (RMSNorm) that scales without centring.

slides.notes:
Expectation and variance are not only for dice. The published transformer design uses layer normalisation, a step from a 2016 paper by Ba, Kiros and Hinton. Inside a layer, each vector of numbers is shifted by its own mean and divided by its own standard deviation. That keeps the numbers in a friendly range, which helps training.

The vector is the whole list, nothing is estimated from a sample, so the published step divides by n, the population form. Some newer open models, Llama among them, use a variant called RMSNorm that scales without centring.

title.text: Exit check: three questions

rows.text: A model gives probabilities 0.5, 0.3 and 0.1 to three words and nothing else is possible. What is wrong?
They add to 0.9. A pmf must add to exactly 1.
Two fair dice are independent. What is P(both show 1)?
Two columns have correlation 0.02. Are they unrelated?
Not necessarily. Correlation only sees straight-line trends. Draw the scatter plot.

slides.notes:
Three questions to finish. First, three words with probabilities 0.5, 0.3 and 0.1 and nothing else possible: they add to 0.9, so something is missing, and a probability mass function must add to exactly one. Second, for two independent dice the probability that both show one is the product, one sixth times one sixth, one thirty-sixth.

Third, correlation near zero does not mean no relationship, because correlation only sees straight lines, so draw the scatter plot. Write your answers in your lab file.
